newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEP seeks consensus on controversial forest policy.
newsitem.headline: MEP seeks consensus on controversial forest policy.

text.p: The European Commission is likely to have a hard time drafting a strategy for managing the European Union's forests, if the experience of MEP David Thomas is anything to go by.

For the last two years Thomas, a British Socialist, has been striving to produce recommendations for an EU forestry policy which satisfy MEPs and interest groups of widely divergent, and strongly held, persuasions.

The result is a draft report, due to be approved by the Euroepan Parliament on Thursday, which tries to find a balance between promoting the timber industry -- a source of jobs and wealth -- and protecting natural resources for future generations.
The report acknowledges that atmospheric pollution and many other causes of forest degradation are problems which transcend national borders and urges the EU to tackle them.
It also says more needs to be done to ensure forests are managed sustainably, without going into details.
But in the wake of protests from various quarters, the report insists that any plans to coordinate national forestry policies must respect subsidiarity.
"The Nordic countries think they have the best policy and European policy would be a dilution," Stefan Leiner of the World Wide Fund for Nature told Reuters.
But WWF insists that even the Scandinavians have a less than perfect record.

Finnish logging companies, for example, continued to cut into areas of protected forest and lay waste large tracts of Russia's Karelian green belt, one of the last remaining ancient forests in northern Europe, Leiner said.

Thomas told Reuters he had personally wanted the report to put more emphasis on the need to protect forest resources, which include not only different species of treeS, but also other plants, animals and insects, as well as valuable soil and water resources.
But he said it had only been possible to get the approval of the European Parliament's agriculture committee by toning down the report's environmental demands.
Thomas said the report -- a parliament initiative -- had succeeded in its main aim of getting the Commission to promise proposals on a forest strategy within two years.
There would be plenty of opportunity to amend these proposals if necessary, he added.
For their part, the WWF and the London-based Environmental Investigation Agency say they are disappointed the parliament appears unable to come up with strong proposals for the Commission to work on.
Thomas' report asks the Commission to tackle in detail a number of thorny issues which MEPs have raised but on which there is no consensus.
These include an internationally recognised system of certificates for sustainably produced timber, and a global forest agreement to prevent illegal and unsustainable logging.
"I support the idea of certification but then you hit upon the argument of whether it should be compulsory or voluntary, and what system you should have," Thomas explained.
His report advocates a legally binding international forest convention which would prevent timber companies shifting operations to countries with lax environmental and social laws.
But he said he understood WWF's fear that governments might be tempted to use the argument that they are negotiating such an agreement to ignore their existing international commitments.

The report also urges the EU to promote the use of more wood products but, partially because of the need to get a consensus in parliament's vote on Thursday, it does not specify that they should come from sustainably managed forests.
Thomas said he hoped the Commission would be able to make more specific recommendations on sustainability.

WWF's Leiner said he hoped these would include restrictions on clear (mass) cutting, unneccessary access roads, large monocultures of species like eucalyptus, wasteful consumption and the use of old-growth or tropical woods for paper and pulp.
